newsitem.title: Portugal: Russia presses summit to strike Serbia criticism.
newsitem.headline: Russia presses summit to strike Serbia criticism.

text.p: Russia defended Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic at a European security summit on Tuesday, insisting on striking out a call for Serbian democracy from a final declaration, a senior Western diplomat said.

A draft of the final communique of the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) summit, due to be issued on Tuesday, had made clear that the meeting believed democracy, an independent media and free elections in Yugoslavia were vital to stability in the Balkans.

Overnight, diplomats laboured over another draft and when the text emerged the sentence -- "Democratisation, independent media, free and fair elections are critical to fostering lasting stability in the area" -- had disappeared.
"Yes, the Russians are behind this," a senior Western diplomat told Reuters.

The change would considerably water down any criticism of Belgrade from the summit at a time when opposition and student demonstrators were on the streets in the biggest protest against Milosevic's nine-year rule.
International peace coordinator Carl Bildt joined Britain and France on Monday to express "deep concern" over a government threat to crack down on the two weeks of protests.
The draft of the final communique merely says that the OSCE should involve itself in accelerating democratisation, promoting an independent media and ensuring free elections.
"The Russians have been insistent and eloquent defenders of the unfortunate Yugoslav position," one Western diplomatic source said.

U.S. Assistant Secretary of State for European and Canadian Affairs John Kornblum, attending the Lisbon summit, said he had voiced Washington's concerns over the internal situation in Serbia on his recent visits to Belgrade.
"I have personally over the past several months been making our concerns over the political, and the economic, situation in Serbia very clear to Milosevic," Kornblum told a news conference.
Because of those worries, the United States had made no move to normalise relations with Belgrade, Kornblum added.
"We can't really expect there to be any long-term stability in the Balkans if Serbia wishes to move backwards," he said.
German Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel said the European Union should take into account the recent political developments in Serbia before authorising EU aid to Belgrade.
"We are very worried about the developments in Serbia," Kinkel told a news conference.
Yugoslavia was suspended from the OSCE body in 1992 after being accused of stoking the war in neighbouring Bosnia.
Russia wants Yugoslavia to be readmitted to the organisation following the Dayton agreement that ended the 43-month war in Bosnia and the lifting of most sanctions against Belgrade.

Many OSCE nations, particularly Bosnia, Croatia and Slovenia, insist Yugoslavia -- now comprising just Serbia and Montenegro -- must reapply for membership to the body, arguing it is no longer the same country as before, a position Belgrade dismisses.
The question of succession is also complicating talks on the resolution of former Yugoslavia's debts and assets among the former Yugoslav republics.
